*A transcript recovered from the Hall of Small Repairs*

**Present:** Archmage Veyra, Keeper of the Scroll of Fates · Magister Orin the Cautious · Healer-Sage Mirelle · Bramblewick, Warden of the Green · The Keeper of the Ledger · Pell, Apprentice (taking notes, mostly)

---

**VEYRA:** The boy asks what the shears are for. Let him ask aloud.

**PELL:** I've read the scrolls, Archmage. A spell that cuts any page in any book, in any library, on demand. That sounds less like magic than like a rumor.

**VEYRA:** It began as a rumor — in bacteria, of all places. Salt-and-iron scribes no bigger than a speck, who kept a memory of every plague that ever tried to eat them, and carried enchanted shears to match. When a familiar plague returned, the scribe unrolled a strip of memory, laid it against the intruder's page, and cut. *(She taps the table.)* We did not invent the shears. We learned to write the address on them.

**PELL:** The address?

**VEYRA:** Twenty letters or so. That is the whole of the guidance — a short strip of code that matches the place you mean to cut and nowhere else. The shears themselves are blind. They cut where the strip points, provided they are granted entry by a small password the page itself must display — a door-knock the old scrolls call the **PAM**. No knock, no cut. It is not a spell that finds its target by wanting to. It is a spell that finds its target by *matching*.

**MIRIELLE:** And matching is why I trust it more than the old fire-charms, and less than the boy hopes.

**PELL:** Less?

**MIRIELLE:** Because the shears cut *both* strands of the page. Always. That is the one certainty. What happens after is the whole of the art.

**VEYRA:** Two roads, Pell. The first: the scribes of the body, seeing a clean break, glue the ends back together in haste — and in haste they drop or duplicate a few letters. Do that inside a sentence and you have smashed the sentence. That is not a failure. That is a *technique*. We call it a knockout: we break the instruction, and the body stops making the thing the instruction made.

**MIRIELLE:** It is how the sickle-cell cure works. *(She turns to the Ledger.)* Not by rewriting the faulty blood-page at all. There is a second, better scroll the body stops reading in infancy — and a warden-glyph that keeps it closed. Break the warden, and the good scroll opens by itself. That cure has passed the trials of the great colleges and is licensed for the sick. It is real. It is expensive. We will come back to that.

**ORIN:** *(dryly)* We will come back to it for some while.

**VEYRA:** The second road is the finer one. Instead of gluing, we hand the scribes a **template** — a corrected copy of the passage — and let them copy it in. Neat, precise, and maddeningly rare. The body prefers haste to accuracy. So the craft has grown cleverer: the **chemist's pencil**, which alters a single letter without ever cutting both strands; and the **searcher's note**, which nicks one strand, writes the replacement directly from a written instruction, and withdraws. *(She smiles.)* Find, replace, done. No break at all.

**PELL:** Then why not use that for everything?

**ORIN:** Because the shears are not the hard part, boy. The *delivery* is.

---

**ORIN:** A spell that works perfectly in a dish is a spell nobody has yet cast. You must get the shears into the right room, of the right house, in the right city — and only those rooms. Send them in a coach and some coaches are turned away at the gate. Send them too many times and the body's guard learns the coach and burns it. Edit a thousand cells and you have cured a thousand cells; the ten million you missed go on as they were.

**MIRIELLE:** And there is a stranger hazard. Edit a body's ordinary cells and the change dies with the patient. Edit the *seed* — the embryo, the germline — and every page copied from it carries the change, forever, into people who never consented to being edited.

**ORIN:** Which is the bright line of this entire council, and I will not have it blurred by enthusiasm. There was a man in the east who crossed it, quietly, to make children. He was not a pioneer. He was a criminal, and the whole guild disowned him.

**PELL:** *(writing fast)* Somatic — the patient. Germline — the bloodline.

**ORIN:** Precisely. One is medicine. The other is rewriting the printing press because you dislike a word in one book.

**VEYRA:** And even in medicine, the shears sometimes nick the wrong page. The address is twenty letters; a wrong page may share eighteen. Read the whole library afterward, or you have not been careful — you have been lucky. *(She raises a hand.)* Do not let the boy leave thinking this is a blade without a handle. It is *measurably* precise. It is not *perfectly* precise. Those are different claims and only one of them is honest.

---

**BRAMBLEWICK:** *(who has been chewing a stem this whole time)* You're all very gloomy about a tool that could feed a continent.

**ORIN:** Warden.

**BRAMBLEWICK:** Blight-resistant grain. Cattle that don't grow horns, so no one saws them off. Oilseed that tolerates a hard summer. Every harvest is already an edit — ten thousand years of the slowest possible craft, and we called it farming. This is the same work with the waiting removed.

**MIRIELLE:** Provided the change stays where you put it, and the field stays where you put it.

**BRAMBLEWICK:** Aye. And provided we're honest about the other thing, the one that keeps me up. *(He sets the stem down.)* You can write a spell that *spreads*. A change that copies itself into every child, and every child's children, until a whole species carries it. We could make the fever-mosquitoes unable to carry the fever. Empty the biting swarms from a coast. Save, by some counts, a great many children a year.

**ORIN:** Or drive a species to nothing because we were certain, at one council, in one season.

**BRAMBLEWICK:** Aye. That too. *(A pause.)* We haven't cast that one. Not in the wild. Not yet.

---

**LEDGER:** May I say the unpopular thing.

**VEYRA:** You always do.

**LEDGER:** The shears will not be distributed by wisdom. They will be distributed by price. A cure that costs a fortune is not a cure for the poor who need it most — it is a very expensive demonstration that a cure is possible. And the small edits, the ones that could matter to millions, are not the ones the coin pursues. The coin pursues the rare and the lucrative. *(She closes her book.)* Every council I have sat in has ended with a marvel, and a queue, and an argument about who stands at the front of it.

**MIRIELLE:** Then we fund the queue.

**LEDGER:** Then we fund the queue.

---

**PELL:** *(after a moment)* So what do I write? That it's a miracle, or that it's a hazard?

**VEYRA:** Neither. Write this. *(She recites, and he writes.)*

> The shears are not intelligent. They are addressed.
> The address is short, and short addresses can be misread.
> The cut is certain; the repair is not, and the repair is where the art lives.
> Delivery decides everything, and delivery is the least magic part of all.
> A change to a body is a treatment. A change to a seed is a lineage. The second is not ours to grant.
> Precision is a measurement, not a promise.
> And a tool that only the wealthy can afford has not solved the problem it was built for.

**ORIN:** Add one line.

**VEYRA:** *(a beat)* Add: *Humility is not the absence of power. It is the correct response to it.*

**PELL:** And the shears themselves? What do I call them in the title?

**VEYRA:** Call them by their true name. **Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats.** *(She sighs.)* The scribes who named them were not poets. Call them CRISPR, and tell the reader plainly that it is a pair of microscopic scissors with a written address — no more, and no less — and that everything wondrous and everything dangerous about it follows from those two small facts.

**BRAMBLEWICK:** *(to Pell, quietly, as the council rises)* And tell them the council argued. That's the part they always leave out of the scrolls.

---

## The Apprentice's Notes

**The shears** — Cas9, a protein that cuts DNA. **The address** — a short guide RNA (about 20 letters) that base-pairs with the target. **The door-knock** — the PAM, a short sequence (NGG for the common *Streptococcus pyogenes* Cas9) that must sit next to the target; it limits which sites can be cut.

**Blunt gluing** — non-homologous end joining (NHEJ): fast, error-prone; used deliberately to knock out a gene. **Copying in a template** — homology-directed repair (HDR): precise but inefficient, mostly in dividing cells. **The chemist's pencil** — base editors (C→T, A→G), which change single letters without a double-strand break. **The searcher's note** — prime editing, which writes in a new sequence from a built-in template.

**Somatic vs germline** — editing body cells affects only the patient; editing embryos or germ cells is heritable. Heritable human editing is prohibited in most countries and was condemned worldwide after He Jiankui's 2018 experiment.

**Already in the clinic** — Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), approved in late 2023, treats sickle cell disease by editing a regulatory switch (the *BCL11A* enhancer) in a patient's own blood stem cells, ex vivo, so that fetal haemoglobin is produced again. Cancer immunotherapies, inherited blindness and amyloidosis trials, and agricultural traits are in various stages behind it.

**Gene drives** — CRISPR constructs that copy themselves through a wild population; powerful for malaria control, and un-deployed in the wild for exactly the reasons Bramblewick gave.

**The honest caveats** — delivery to the right tissue, immune responses, mosaicism in embryos, off-target edits, unknown long-term effects, ecological risk, and cost. CRISPR is a precise tool, not a self-directing one — which is why the argument in that council is the most important part of the technology."}
